title.en: The Wolf and the Sheep, His Aunt

region.en: Forest edge of a hill village (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 山村林緣（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXIX, The Wolf and the Sheep (Kah-gyur iv. 287)

summary.en: A lagging old ewe is seized by a wolf who greets her as 'aunt' and accuses her of pinching and plucking his tail; the sheep answers that his tail spreads over the four parts of the world, so she must have come through the air - which the wolf turns into a fresh accusation, that her flying scared away the gazelles he meant to feed on, and he tears off her head.
summary.zh: 掉隊的老母羊被狼咬住；狼呼其為「姨母」，指控她扯拔己尾。羊答「你之尾遍佈四洲，我必是從空中飛來的」；狼反咬一口：「你飛天時驚散了我欲食的羚羊群」，遂撕裂羊首食其肉。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The wolf asked whether she thought she would escape after pinching his tail and plucking hairs out of it; the sheep answered, how could I pinch your tail, seeing it is behind you and I have been going in front? 'Which way then did you come,' said the wolf, 'seeing that my tail spreads all over the four parts of the world, together with the ocean and the hill-villages?' 'As I had heard beforehand from my kinsmen that your tail spreads everywhere, I came through the air.' 'If you came through the air, you must have scared away the herd of gazelles which I meant to feed upon.' Having thus spoken the malefactor made a spring, tore off the sheep's head, and devoured its flesh.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Wolf and the Sheep (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Oxen as Witnesses: Breakstump Before the King
title.zh: 牛為證：斷角殘尾對王庭

region.en: Corn-field and royal court of a hill district (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 山地田疇與王廷（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXX, Oxen as Witnesses (Kah-gyur vi. 228-231)

summary.en: An orphan youth ploughs faithfully for a householder who promises him his daughter, breaks an ox's horn and tail in temper and names the beast Breakstump, then is put off harvest after harvest and reviled as a day-labourer. In those days, not long after the creation of the world, even brute beasts could speak: his oxen offer themselves as witnesses, prescribing the ordeal - tied up seven days without grass or water, then freed, to prove his truth by refusing both so long as the king doubts. Breakstump alone must be bridled by his nose, held up toward the sun, 'the fifth guardian of the world, is also a witness.'
summary.zh: 孤兒青年為田主耕作，田主許婚而不踐，屢以農事推託，又罵他為雇工。彼時離開天闢地不久，獸類尚能言語：雙牛自願為證，授以考驗之法——縛七日不給草水，第七日縱之於草水豐美處，若青年所言屬實，牛即不食不飲直至王信。頑牛「斷角殘尾」被同伴以角托鼻仰日：「日為世界第五守護者，亦是見證。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The youth, wronged of his promised bride, left the oxen tied to a dry tree in the sun; they spoke to him - for it was part of the nature of things, not long after the creation of the world, that even brute beasts could speak - and on hearing his story prescribed the ordeal: tie us in our stalls for seven days without grass or water, then let us go free to a place where both are plentiful, and say to the king, 'if I am speaking the truth may these oxen neither eat grass nor drink water.' The king agreed to the test.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Oxen as Witnesses (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Breakstump alone threatened to eat even stones if freed, for his master's son had named him so; the youth, advised by the other oxen, bored his nose, and on the seventh day, as Breakstump stooped to grass, his fellows seized his nose with their horns and looked up toward the sun. Asked why the oxen looked up, a minister said it was to show that the sun, the fifth guardian of the world, was also a witness. The king wondered, and the householder, overcome, bestowed his daughter on the young man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Oxen as Witnesses (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Stubborn and the Willing Oxen

region.en: Forest road to watered meadows (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 林間道路至水草之地（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXI, The Stubborn and the Willing Oxen (Kah-gyur iv. 248-249)

summary.en: Two merchant caravans rest exhausted oxen at a meadow rich in grass and water. The lead-ox of one troop counsels staying forever; the lead-ox of the other counsels bearing the burden, since men are strong and masters of the difficult-to-subdue. Called a coward, the second troop's ox retorts that none has seen the farther side of the moon - and when loading comes, the stubborn are beaten, lacerated with thorny rods and yoked dripping with blood, while the willing suffer no harm.
summary.zh: 兩支商隊的牛在水草豐美處歇息。一隊頭牛主張永留此地；另一隊頭牛主張負重前行——「人力強大，能制服難馭之物，不如忍受重擔」。對方怒斥「誰見過月亮背面」，堅不負重；結果裝載之時，倔牛被鞭打、棘杖撕裂、血染而駕轅，順牛則安然無損。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The leading ox of the second troop counseled enduring the burden, since men are strong and have the mastery over even the difficult to be subdued; the first chief ox answered angrily that none has seen the further side of the moon, and his troop would not endure theirs. When the merchants loaded their oxen, the first set held stubbornly back and were beaten, lacerated with thorny rods, and yoked dripping with blood; the others submitted to the yoke without resisting, so no harm came to them. A deity sang: see how the steers which the ox misguided, bleeding and wounded, suffer hunger and thirst.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Stubborn and the Willing Oxen (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ass as a Singer

region.en: King's bean-field outside the city (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 城外王豆田（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXII, The Ass as a Singer (Kah-gyur iv. 293)

summary.en: The Bodhisattva, born a bull, feeds nightly in the king's bean-field; an ass joins him, promising not to raise his voice. Silent till full, the ass then asks leave to sing a little - the bull runs off, the ass sings, the king's men seize him and punish the 'devourer of the bean-field' by cutting off his ears and fastening a pestle to his neck. Bull and ass trade parting verses about recompense and three men searching with clubs.
summary.zh: 菩薩生為公牛，每夜入王豆田覓食；一驢同行，允諾不出聲。飽食之後驢要求「唱一小曲」，牛奔逃，驢高歌——王之人擒驢，罰其「吃光豆田」：割去雙耳，頸繫木杵而釋之。牛驢互誦偈語而別。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Inside the bean-field the ass uttered no sound until it had eaten its fill, then asked, uncle, shall not I sing a little? The bull replied, wait until I have gone away, then do as you please; and as soon as the ass lifted up its voice the king's people seized it and, to punish the devourer of the bean-field, cut off its ears, fastened a pestle to its neck, and set it free. The bull saw it wandering and pronounced his verse: excellently hast thou sung, and therefore obtained thy recompense - to wander adorned with a club and destitute of ears. The ass retorted: keep silence, thou with broken teeth, for three men are searching for thee with clubs in their hands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Ass as a Singer (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Jackal Sets Lion and Bull at Variance

region.en: Lair and meadow of a great forest (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 大森林之獸穴與草場（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXIII A, The Jackal as Calumniator (Kah-gyur vi. 239-243)

summary.en: A lioness kills a cow for her unborn cub and rears the cow's calf beside her own, charging both, as they had sucked the same dugs, to be brothers and never listen to calumniators. An old remainder-devouring jackal, seeing in the bull the rival of his maw, tells each that the other plans to eat him, prophesying the other's stretching, yawning, triple roar. When the prophesied gestures happen - natural acts never before noticed - both believe the lie, close, and destroy each other: the lion grips the bull's breast, the bull slits the lion's belly.
summary.zh: 母獅獵牛為胎兒備食，連牛犢一併哺乳，臨終囑二人「同乳為兄弟，勿聽讒言」。老豺視牛為爭食之敵，向彼此謊稱對方欲食己，並預言其伸腰、呵欠、三嘯之兆。兆果應驗——本是天性之舉，從未留意——雙方各信讒言，獅攫牛胸，牛角裂獅腹，兩敗俱亡。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; this is the Siddhi-Kur story-type noted by Benfey.

passages.text: The jackal, seeing the lion playing with the bull, judged the bull the adversary of his maw and resolved to set the comrades at variance. With drooping ears he told the bull that the lion had asked, 'whither has gone the bull which belongs to my stores of flesh? If I find no other flesh, I shall devour that bull'; and he told the lion that the bull had vowed, 'as his mother killed my mother, I will slit up his belly.' Each cited the dying mother's warning, but each was taught the prophecy of the other's stretching, yawning and triple roar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal as Calumniator (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Both animals had always acted so according to their natures without ever taking notice; but now the seed of discord was sown. The lion came forth from his lair, stretched, yawned, looked round on all four sides and roared three times; the bull came from the meadow, stretched, bellowed, tore up the ground and snorted. Each thought the other meant murder; the lion seized the bull's breast with his claws, the bull slit up the lion's belly with his horns, and so they both perished. A deity sang: men who pay regard to what is good ought not to hold converse with bad men - see how the jackal set at variance the lion and the bull who had been friends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal as Calumniator (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tricked Elephant

region.en: Bathing pool of an elephant herd (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 象群浴池（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXVIII, The Tricked Elephant (Kah-gyur iv. 256)

summary.en: A she-elephant in love with another male tricks her admirer into a diving contest - who can stay longest under water - and flees with her lover while he holds his breath. Surfacing, he thinks she has beaten him, dives again, props himself on the bottom with his tusks, and in his rage tramples fishes, frogs and tortoises - 'what a huge lump of flesh devoid of intelligence! because another has carried off the female, he inflicts injury upon others.'
summary.zh: 母象另有所愛，誘追求者比賽潛水；趁他閉氣，與情郎逃走。他浮起不見母象，以為輸了，再潛以牙撐底；出水後狂怒亂踏，殃及魚蛙龜——「無智之巨肉！因他人奪其所愛，遂傷無辜。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: She invited him into the pool to see which of them could remain under water the longest; as soon as he, liberally endowed with stupidity, had gone under along with her, she emerged and fled with the young elephant. When he emerged at last and found her gone, he thought he was in danger of being surpassed, went under again, and propped himself up at the bottom with his tusks. Out of breath at last, he tramped wildly about the tank, inflicting unjustifiable injury on fishes, frogs, tortoises and many other creatures - and a deity sang what a huge lump of flesh devoid of intelligence, because another has carried off the female he inflicts injury upon others.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Tricked Elephant (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Flight of the Beasts

region.en: Vilva forest by a lake (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 湖畔菴羅林（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXII, The Flight of the Beasts (Kah-gyur vii. 194)

summary.en: A vilva tree falls into a lake with a great noise; six hares flee, and the panic propagates through jackals, monkeys, gazelles, boars, buffaloes, rhinoceroses, elephants, bears, hyaenas, panthers, tigers and lions, each new species running on the word 'there was a noise'. A maned lion at the mountain's foot stops the rout by demanding the chain of hearsay back to the hares, who show him the fallen tree - 'that was only an empty sound'; a deity sings that men ought to see everything for themselves.
summary.zh: 一株菴羅樹轟然墜湖；六兔奔逃，訊息以「有巨響」一語層層傳播——豺、猴、羚、豬、牛、犀、象、熊、鬣狗、豹、虎、獅相繼狂奔。山腳鬃獅喝止眾獸，逐一追問傳言之源，直至目擊的兔子引路看樹：「不過是空響而已。」天神唱言：人當親見，勿信空言。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The panic passed from hares through jackals, monkeys, gazelles, boars, buffaloes, rhinoceroses, elephants, bears, hyaenas, panthers, tigers and lions, each new troop asking why the others ran and taking flight on hearing only 'there was a noise'. At the mountain's foot a maned lion demanded: do not run - inquiry must be made as to where the noise came from; he asked each species who had told them, down the chain to the hares.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Flight of the Beasts (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hares led him to the vilva forest and showed the fallen tree whose crash had made the noise; the lion said, be not afraid, for that was only an empty sound, and all were tranquillised. A deity uttered the verse: let not men believe in words; they ought to see everything for themselves - observe how, through the fall of a vilva, the forest lost its beasts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Flight of the Beasts (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Five Lovers in the Fig-Tree
title.zh: 無花果樹上的五位情人

region.en: Great fig-tree outside a city (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 城外大無花果樹（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXIII, The Five Lovers (Kah-gyur ix. 67-69)

summary.en: A merchant's wife strings along four stipendiaries and their superior officer, stationing each on a different branch of a great fig-tree for a night meeting she never keeps; bound by her husband, she stays away, and the five pass the dawn composing verses of self-reproach while the tree-deity mocks them. Later she promises herself to whoever brings the most beautiful flowers; four flatter the mutilated keeper of the king's lotuses with nonsense about noses growing back - the fifth tells the truth - and the truthful one wins her.
summary.zh: 商人之妻周旋於四吏與其上司之間，分派各上大無花果樹不同枝椏幽會；她被丈夫捆縛失約，五人徹夜在風中作詩自嘲，樹神亦譏之。後她許諾獻花最美者可得其身；四人對鼻耳被割的蓮花看守大唱恭維胡謅，唯第五人直言「割掉便不會再長」，看守遂以蓮花酬誠實者。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Each lover was stationed by the woman's instruction on a different branch - east, south, west, north and the middle - and they spent the whole night in expectation, terrified by the wind, while the woman never came. As day dawned each composed a verse of complaint, and the deity dwelling in the tree mocked them: you will complain, and the four others too - when the Vaisakha month comes, the tree which men have maimed recovers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Five Lovers (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: She promised herself to whichever of them brought the most beautiful flowers, and they went to the keeper of the king's lotuses, whose nose and ears had been cut off. Four praised him with absurd flattery - as the bulrush grows again after being cut, so may your nose grow again - but the fifth said plainly: the lotus-cravers have all talked nonsense to you; whether you give lotuses or do not, your nose will never grow again. The keeper judged the four had talked useless stuff and the fifth had kept steadily to the truth, and gave him as many lotuses as he wanted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Five Lovers (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Virtuous Animals and the Five Vows

region.en: Fig-tree grove near Varanasi (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈附近的榕林（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXIV, The Virtuous Animals (Kah-gyur iii. 189-193)

summary.en: A partridge, hare, monkey and elephant live in amity and settle precedence by the fig-tree's age - the partridge dropped the seed - then take the five vows one by one (no killing, no taking the unbestowed, no unlawful union, no falsehood, no intoxicating fruits) and carry them to every creature of the Kasi land. Rain falls, seeds and fruit-trees abound, the king traces the blessing to the four animals through a diviner Rishi, adopts the five vows, and half of Jambudvipa follows him to rebirth in Tushita - where the Buddha reveals he was the partridge, Sariputra the hare, Maudgalyayana the monkey, Ananda the elephant.
summary.zh: 鷓鴣、兔、猿、象和合而居，以榕樹年齡定尊卑（鷓鴣播種），隨後逐一受持五戒（不殺、不取、不邪淫、不妄語、不飲酒），並教化迦尸國一切生靈。時雨順調、五穀豐登，國王經仙人占問得知福由四獸，遂行五戒，閻浮提大半隨之生兜率天——佛陀自言：彼時鷓鴣是我，兔是舍利弗，猿是目犍連，象是阿難。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; the Tittira Jataka type; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: To settle precedence the animals examined the fig-tree: the elephant saw it the size of his body, the monkey of his own, the hare licked dew from two leaves - but the partridge had eaten the seed from which the tree sprang, so he was the oldest, and each paid reverence to his elders. Riding each other in the forest - partridge on hare on monkey on elephant - they took up the five vows in turn: not to put living creatures to death, not to take the unbestowed, not to enter unlawful unions, not to speak at random, and to give up intoxicating fruits.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Virtuous Animals (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Duly set fast in the five vows, they confirmed all creatures of the animal world in them, and their influence brought timely rain and seeds, flowers and fruit-trees without end. The king of the land, told by a diviner Rishi that the blessing came from four living creatures, learned the five vows from him, adopted them with all his realm, and the greater part of Jambudvipa followed - whosoever died then was born again in the Tushita region of the thirty-three gods. Bhagavant said: I myself was the partridge of that period; the hare was Sariputra, the monkey Maudgalyayana, and the elephant Ananda.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Virtuous Animals (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ichneumon, the Mouse, and the Snake

region.en: Mouse-hole in the rain (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雨中鼠穴（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXV, The Ichneumon, the Mouse, and the Snake (Kah-gyur iv. 213-214)

summary.en: Rain for seven unseasonable days drives an ichneumon, a mouse and a snake into one hole, where they swear mutual peace. Sent to forage, the honest mouse Gangadatta finds nothing, and the ichneumon Nanda plots to eat him on his return; the snake Nandasena, judging character truly, warns Gangadatta - who sends back word that one weakened by hunger becomes merciless, and Gangadatta will return no more.
summary.zh: 反常大雨七日，獴、鼠、蛇同避一穴，互誓相安。誠實的鼠迦那達受命覓食無果；獴難陀謀劃空手而歸即食之；蛇難陀塞那洞察其心，先行告知——鼠回言「飢餓使人無情，迦那達不再回來」。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The snake, who was named Nandasena, said all had suffered the agony of intolerable woe and ought to remain without exposing one another to danger. The honest mouse Gangadatta went stealing for food and found none; Nanda declared that if he came back without food he would eat him, and Nandasena, judging that a creature ready to kill even amid shared anguish would kill for hunger, gave the mouse notice beforehand. Gangadatta sent back word that as one weakened by hunger becomes merciless, Gangadatta will return no more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Ichneumon, the Mouse, and the Snake (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Grateful Animals and the Ungrateful Man
title.zh: 感恩的動物與忘恩的人

region.en: Deep pit in the king's park (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 王苑深坑（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXVI, The Grateful Animals and the Ungrateful (Kah-gyur iv. 212-213)

summary.en: A woodcutter fleeing a lion, a lion chasing him, a mouse fleeing a snake and a falcon chasing the mouse all tumble into one pit, where the lion forbids mutual slaughter until a hunter draws them out one by one - warned by the lion not to spare 'that black-headed one who forgets accepted benefits'. The falcon repays the hunter with a queen's ornaments lost in the park; the ungrateful black-headed man denounces him, and he is bound and cast into prison - until the grateful snake has the king bitten and the hunter cures him with spell and remedy.
summary.zh: 樵夫、獅、鼠、鷂同墮一坑，獅止殺相待；獵人逐一救出——獅警告勿放那忘恩的黑頭人。鷂以王后在苑中遺失的瓔珞報恩；黑頭人卻告發獵人，使其被縛入獄——直到感恩的蛇咬傷國王，獵人以咒與藥治癒，王喜而釋之並加賞賜。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: All four fell into the pit and entertained the evil design of putting each other to death, but the lion said there was no time to expose one another to danger while they suffered intolerable pain. A hunter, looking for gazelles, drew them out one by one; the lion touched his feet and warned him not to draw out that black-headed one who forgets accepted benefits.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Grateful Animals and the Ungrateful (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The falcon, grateful, carried off from the sleeping park a royal wife's ornaments and presented them to the hunter; the black-headed man, visiting the hunter and knowing of them, came with ungrateful heart and told the king. The hunter was bound and cast into prison; then the mouse went to the snake, and the snake had the king bitten so that the hunter might heal him with spell and remedy - the king joyfully released him and bestowed gifts and good things.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Grateful Animals and the Ungrateful (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Woodpecker and the Ungrateful Lion

region.en: Flat rock of the hill forest (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 山林平岩（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXVII, The Ungrateful Lion (Kah-gyur iv. 181)

summary.en: A bone sticks fast between the lion-king's teeth and prostrates him with pain; the woodpecker (the Bodhisattva) extracts it by a continued fluttering of wings while the lion sleeps with open jaws, on a promised return of service. Later, starving, the woodpecker asks for a piece of flesh - and the lion answers in verse that he who passed between my teeth should be thankful for remaining alive. The woodpecker replies that profitless are benefits conferred on the ungrateful.
summary.zh: 獸王牙間卡骨，痛極臥地；啄木鳥（菩薩）趁其張口而眠，鼓翼振翅取出骨頭，約定日後相助。後來啄木鳥飢餓求食，獅卻以偈答「從我齒間過者，活命已當感恩」。鳥答偈：「施恩於忘恩者，徒勞無益。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The lion passed into a happier mood when the pain abated, went to sleep with its jaws apart on a great flat rock, and the woodpecker, by a continued fluttering of its wings, extracted the bone which had stuck between its teeth. Promised a return of service, it flew away; later, having barely escaped a falcon and tormented by hunger, it asked the lion for a piece of flesh - and the lion replied in verse: are not you, who passed between my teeth, thankful for remaining alive? The woodpecker answered likewise in verse: profitless are intercourse with a bad man and benefits conferred on the ungrateful.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Ungrateful Lion (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Marvel Wagers of Mahaushadha's Son

region.en: Feast in the royal park of Videha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 韋提訶王苑宴會（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. VIII, Mahaushadha and Visakha

summary.en: At a feast of marvel-telling, Mahaushadha's son wagers five hundred gold pieces on a floating cornerstone in his father's house; his father forbids showing it and the wager is forfeit. Trained monkeys dancing, singing and drumming are then staked for double - shown at the palace, they win a thousand pieces, and the king marvels that he has never seen the like; the court honors Mahaushadha as wise above all men.
summary.zh: 宴會上眾人誇說奇事，大藥之子以五百金賭家中有一入水浮游之柱基石；父囑勿示人，賭金盡失。隨後受過音樂訓練的猴子能歌善舞擊鼓，以雙倍賭注再賭——猴子入宮獻藝，贏回千金，王嘆未曾目睹，舉朝推尊大藥之智。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Mahaushadha's son staked five hundred pieces of gold on the stone which, though it formed the base of a column, would swim to and fro if thrown into water; his father ordered him not to show the stone, and the wager was forfeit. Later Mahaushadha took monkeys and gave them a musical training, and the son staked twice as much on musical monkeys capable of dancing and singing and playing on the drum.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The monkeys were brought into the royal palace, where they played and sang and danced before the king; the young men were obliged to pay the thousand pieces of gold, and the king, who had never seen or heard anything like it, paid great honour to Mahaushadha as wise and clever above all other men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Virupa the Ugly and Udumbarika the Fair
title.zh: 醜者毘盧巴與美者鄔波摩離迦

region.en: Videha forest and royal park (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 韋提訶林野與王苑（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. VIII, Mahaushadha and Visakha

summary.en: Virupa, marked with eighteen signs of ugliness, masters all learning abroad and wins the learned Brahman's beautiful daughter Udumbarika - who is ashamed of him. Starving on the road, he denies her meat, blood and ripe fruit, citing the Rishis' ban on women; then he rings her tree with thorns and walks away, and King Janaka, hearing her wailing in the forest, takes her to wife. Virupa creeps into the palace as a stone-carrier and challenges his wife in verses; Mahaushadha resolves the tangle by assembling the king's five hundred women and letting Virupa identify his wife - and the frightened Brahman seizes a water-carrier, crying 'the crooked one loves the crooked one.'
summary.zh: 醜陋的毘盧巴學成於外，娶得博學婆羅門之美女鄔波摩離迦，卻遭她嫌棄。路上斷糧，他以「仙人禁女人」為由獨享肉、血與熟果，後更以棘刺圍樹棄妻而去。闍那迦王聞林中悲泣，納她為妃。毘盧巴扮搬石工人混入王宮，與妻以偈對答；大藥獻策聚五百嬪妃令其指認，嚇破膽的婆羅門竟抓住一名挑水婢喊「曲者愛曲者」。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; the tale's treatment of the wife belongs to its narrative frame, reported factually.

passages.text: Starving on the road, Virupa roasted dog's flesh found in the drought and refused his wife any, because the early Rishis had forbidden women to partake of such food; at a ripe Udumbara tree he ate the fruit himself and threw down only what was unripe, telling her to climb and pluck if she wanted ripe fruit. When she had climbed in torment of hunger, he surrounded the tree with thorns and went his way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: King Janaka, hunting, heard the wailing of Udumbarika deserted by her husband, seemed to see a goddess of the forest, and took her to the city as one of his wives. Virupa, repenting, got into the palace by carrying stone with the workmen and challenged his wife in verses - she answered every verse with the memory of 'to women meat is forbidden' and the unripe fruit. Mahaushadha proposed the identification ordeal: pick out your wife from among five hundred - if you choose one who does not belong to you, your body shall be cut to pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: All the king's wives appeared in full bravery, Udumbarika at their head like the spouse of Indra; Virupa stood still like a snake charmed by a spell, then saw a female slave, a carrier of water, like a Pisachi at the back, seized her hand and cried, this is my wife. He took her away with the words, the excellent loves the excellent, and the mediocre the mediocre; I am like unto a Pisacha, and you too are a Pisachi - come unto me. Therefore King Janaka forgave Mahaushadha all the faults he had ever committed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Pearl Necklace and the Dancing Monkey

region.en: Asoka grove of the royal park (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 王苑阿輸迦樹林（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. VIII, Mahaushadha and Visakha

summary.en: A queen hangs a hundred-thousand-pearl string on an asoka spray and forgets it; a she-monkey carries it to the tree-top. An innocent beggar is beaten and jailed for the theft, and dines his way through accused companions - merchant, courtesan, lute-player - until he names Mahaushadha's son to summon the minister. Mahaushadha frees them all on his word, finds the monkey, and stages the recovery: the queen wears a necklace and dances, the monkey imitates her - and when she is told to dance with head hanging down, the pearl string drops from the monkey's neck.
summary.zh: 王后把十萬珠鏈掛上阿輸迦枝而忘卻，被母猴攜上樹頂。無辜乞兒被屈打成招下獄，先後把商人、妓女、琴師一一「攀」進獄中同享飯食，直至點名大藥之子。大藥一句擔保救出全部囚犯，繼而請王后戴鏈起舞，猴在樹頂模仿；王后垂首而舞，猴亦垂首，珠鏈應聲落下。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The beggar, jailed for a theft he never saw, gained food by accusing a young merchant, then a courtesan, then a lute-player, and at last named Mahaushadha's son, so that the ministers summoned him also. Mahaushadha told the king the theft had not been committed by any of these people and had them all freed on his word.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: He went to the very tree, saw the she-monkey at the top, and asked the king to go there with his wife and hang a necklace round her neck. The monkey hung the pearl necklace round its own; told to dance, the queen danced and the monkey danced too, but the string did not fall - until Mahaushadha asked the queen to dance with her head hanging down, and the monkey, dancing with head hanging down, let the string of pearls drop from its neck. The king embraced Mahaushadha and bestowed much property on him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Six Ministers' Oath and the Parrot's Ear

region.en: Park grove of Videha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 韋提訶苑林（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. VIII, Mahaushadha and Visakha

summary.en: Stripped of credit by a half-starved upstart, the six ministers go into the park to swear mutual support, confessing their secrets one by one - I ate the king's peacock; I sinned with the king's wife; I will do likewise - and partaking of one vessel. Mahaushadha, suspecting the rendezvous, sends the parrot Mathara after them, hears everything, reports to the king, and the ministers are banished from the country.
summary.zh: 六相因失寵於出身寒微的首輔，相約入林盟誓互助，互吐隱情——「我吃了王的孔雀」「我與王妃有私」「我也要如此」——並共食一器。大藥疑其聚謀，遣鸚鵡摩多羅隨行竊聽，盡得所言，奏於國王，六相被逐出國境。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Some said: inasmuch as we have hitherto been at variance one with another, we have become destitute of power - let us take an oath and bind ourselves by a vow. In the park they communicated their faults and secrets one to another - I ate the king's peacock, said one; I sinned with the king's wife, said another; I will do likewise, said a third - and partook of food out of the same vessel.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mahaushadha, seeing them go off by common consent, sent the parrot Mathara after them to find out what they said and did; the parrot reported all it had heard, Mahaushadha reported it to the king, and the king banished those ministers from the country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Nyagrodha Tree Deity and the Son of Heaven
title.zh: 尼拘陀樹神與天子下生

region.en: Great Nyagrodha tree of Nyagrodhika city (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼拘陀城的尼拘陀大神樹（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. IX, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra (Kah-gyur ix. 26-42)

summary.en: The childless millionaire Nyagrodha prays to the tree-deity that answered his own father, threatening to fell, split, burn and scatter the tree if no son is granted. The frightened deity appeals up the chain of heaven - to Rashtrapala, the four Maharajas, Sakra, none competent, since sons are born of their own merits - until Mahabrahma appears, whose very titles would be discredited by refusal. Inspecting his region for a dying god, Brahma commands one into the Brahman's house despite the god's protest that Brahmans' perverse doctrines are golden fetters - and the god's son is born as Nyagrodhaja, later called Kasyapa.
summary.zh: 巨富婆羅門無子，向助其父得子的尼拘陀樹神祈求，並以砍碎焚揚相威脅。樹神懼而逐級上告——四天王、帝釋皆言子嗣由宿業所定，不能賜予——直至大梵天現身，若拒絕則其種種尊號皆將落空。梵天察其界得壽盡之神一名，強令其投生婆羅門家；神雖斥婆羅門邪見如「黃金鎖鏈」，仍受命入胎，生為尼拘陀闍，後名迦葉。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Nyagrodha prayed to the tree-haunting deity: bestow on me a son, and I will pay boundless honour for a year - but if no son is born I will cleave thee down to the level of beard-grass and split thee into chips, burn them dried by wind and sun, and scatter the ashes to the storm-wind. The deity of small power, afraid of being driven from its haunt, appealed to the four Maharajas and to Sakra, all of whom declared that sons and daughters are born only as the result of former actions.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then appeared Mahabrahma in youthful perfection, and Sakra prayed to him by all his titles - Brahma, Mahabrahma, the ruler, the worker, the bestower, the spell-wielder, the most high, father of the worlds, creator of all beings. Brahma reflected that to refuse would discredit every title, and privately confessed to Sakra: neither has the world made me, nor I the world. Inspecting his own region he found a god whose life was ending, five prognostics visible, and commanded him into the Brahman's house; the god protested that he who wishes to be born of a Brahman is like one who from love of golden fetters sets his own feet in bondage, and that the Bodhisattva would soon descend from Tushita as a snow-white six-tusked elephant - but at Brahma's insistence he consented, and the fine boy was born as Nyagrodhaja.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Golden Image and the Goddess of Virgins

region.en: Market-places of the four quarters (symbolic pin at Kapila)
region.zh: 四方集市（以迦毘羅為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. IX, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra

summary.en: To dodge marriage, Kasyapa demands a wife like a gold image; four copies are sent to the four quarters disguised as the Goddess of Virgins, granting five wishes to maidens who worship her. In Kapila the Brahman Kapila's daughter Bhadra, herself without longing for love, approaches the image - and it dulls to iron in her presence, betraying that her radiance outshines gold. The Brahmans' sons win the betrothal with proverbs about fire and firm-resolved Brahmans that cannot be stopped.
summary.zh: 迦葉為逃避婚事，索要一位如金像般的妻子；四尊複製品分赴四方，冒充「處女神」，向禮拜的少女們許諾五願。迦毘羅城的婆羅門女婆陀本無情慾，近前時金像竟黯如鐵——顯見她的光輝勝過黃金。眾婆羅門弟子以「火、風、馬、行血之毒、堅志婆羅門皆不可止」的諺語說服其父訂婚。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Nyagrodhaja had a smith make a woman's likeness out of Jambu-river gold and swore to wed none but her counterpart; his father had three more images made, and the young Brahmans carried them through villages, towns and cities, setting each up as the Goddess of Virgins who grants five wishes to maidens who honour her - birth in an exalted race, marriage into an exalted race, residence in a fully provided house, submission of the husband, and possession of children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Bhadra, the beautiful daughter of the Brahman Kapila, who had no longing after any kind of love, went to make her offering only at her mother's urging; as she drew near, the image became less and less brilliant until it seemed made of iron, for the radiance proceeded from the maiden herself. Asked why they did not want the gift of meal, the Brahmans' sons answered they wanted her, and won Kapila with the saying: fire, wind, a horse, a poison that runs along the veins, and a Brahman of firm resolution, do not allow themselves to be stopped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Twelve Years of One Bed: Kasyapa and Bhadra's Vow
title.zh: 一榻十二載：迦葉與婆陀之誓

region.en: Bridal house of Nyagrodhika (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼拘陀城新房（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. IX, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra

summary.en: Married under a shared vow of continence, the couple sleep by turns on one bed, then walk by turns when the stool too is removed; for twelve years no amorous thought arises. Sakra descends to test them as a poisonous snake under the bed, and Nyagrodhaja lifts his sleeping wife's hand with a fly-flapper's jeweled handle rather than touch her - for which she rebukes him: better the snake should bite me, for as a fair tree clasped by a creeper perishes, so men go to ruin from a woman's touch.
summary.zh: 二人共持貞潔之誓，輪流臥一床；撤去小凳後便輪流步行至明。十二年中二人未起一念情慾。帝釋化身毒蛇藏於床下試探，迦葉以拂柄寶飾一端抬起熟睡妻子的手——她醒而責之：「寧被蛇咬，不願被觸。美樹為藤所纏則枯，男子觸婦人則自毀。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: They admonished one another to remember the vow and lived together like a mother and a son; when one bed was provided, Bhadra slept in the first watch and Nyagrodhaja on the stool, and they alternated through the night. When the stool too was taken away, each slept in turn while the other walked up and down - and thus for twelve years they occupied the same single-bedded room without an amorous thought arising.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king of the gods, Sakra, resolved to test such freedom from passion, assumed the form of a snake with terrible poison fangs, and coiled under the bed; fearing for his sleeping wife's hanging hand, Nyagrodhaja lifted it with the jewelled handle of the fly-flapper. Bhadra awoke crying, surely you have not touched me with amorous intent! - and better would it have been that the snake should have bitten me, for as a fair tree clasped by the maluta creeper perishes, so do men go to ruin from a woman's touch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Kasyapa's Renunciation and the Buddha's Robe

region.en: Penance forest and Bahuputrachaitya (symbolic pin at Rajagriha)
region.zh: 苦行林與多子塔（以王舍城為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. IX, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra

summary.en: Inheriting his father's estates, Kasyapa sees the plough-oxen tortured by insects, the laborers wale-backed and quarrelling like Pisachas for a ploughshare, and resolves to acquire merit by neither sinning in body nor speech; Bhadra, seeing her slave-women the same, empties the household's stores on the poor. Both leave together - she first, that no man may long after the wife 'as after rice-soup ready for the table' - and at Bahuputrachaitya Kasyapa meets the Buddha under a tree, giving him his costly cotton robe and receiving the Buddha's robe in return.
summary.zh: 迦葉視察田莊，見耕牛為蟲所苦、雇工遍體鞭痕如夜叉般爭執，遂誓不再以身口造業；婆陀見婢女亦然，散盡家中財物賑濟貧者。二人一同出家——婆陀先行，免得丈夫走後有人「如盼桌上米粥般」覬覦其妻。於多子塔，迦葉在樹下見佛，以價值十萬的金縷衣供佛，換得佛陀所著之衣。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Nyagrodhaja saw the plough-oxen tormented by insects, their nostrils bored, shoulders worn, loins torn by the iron, and the labourers, covered with dust, like burnt-out tree-stumps, abusing and striking one another for the sake of a plough or a goad - so he resolved to acquire merit by sinning neither with body nor in speech or thought. Bhadra, seeing her slave-women striking each other with pestles on account of mortars, was moved likewise, and bestowed gifts so that the poor were no longer poor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Bhadra begged to go with him into the forest of penance, he objected that it was not allowable to live there with a wife; she answered that she must go first, lest other men long after her as after rice-soup ready for the table, and he judged her discreet. From Venuvana Bhagavant betook himself to Bahuputrachaitya; there Kasyapa saw him under a tree, was received by him, gave him the costly cotton robe, and received the Buddha's robe in return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Bhadra Among the Nirgranthas and the Flying Escape
title.zh: 婆陀在裸形外道中與凌空而脫

region.en: Rajagriha, Nirgrantha quarters and royal palace (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 王舍城裸形外道居地與王宮（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. IX, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra

summary.en: Bhadra enters the clerical order of the Nirgrantha Purana, and five hundred of his pupils, coveting her divine beauty, obtain her from the teacher; the Buddha's wife-to-be Mahaprajapati later receives her into the Buddhist order, and when her beauty draws every eye 'like a fat sheep', Mahakasyapa shares his alms with her daily until she becomes an Arhantin. Then the patricide Ajatasatru, comfortless in sorrow, has her seized from her alms-round; washed, perfumed and adorned, she is given to the king - and when he would embrace her she rises heavenward by magic, letting herself down only when he falls at her feet and begs forgiveness.
summary.zh: 婆陀入裸形外道普蘭那門下，五百弟子貪其美貌而從其師處強索。後由大愛道引入佛教僧團；因其美貌出眾「如肥羊」引人側目，迦葉每日分半缽與之，直至她證阿羅漢果。弒父的阿闍世王悲不自勝，奸臣獻計於乞食途中劫走婆陀，洗浴妝點獻於王；王慾擁之，婆陀以神通凌空而起，王驚懼跪求，方得赦免之諾。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The five hundred Nirgranthas, in consequence of former actions, enjoyed her company every day until, disquieted, she consulted Purana, who said only: whom the lot betokens, with him have to do. Kasyapa, finding her appearance altered at the festival of the Nagarajas, asked whether she had preserved her chastity, and sent her to Mahaprajapati, who received her; when she complained that like a fat sheep she attracted universal attention, he gave her daily half of what he himself collected, until she became an Arhantin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Ajatasatru had killed his father and nothing sufficed to rouse him from his sorrow, an evil minister proposed the beautiful Bhadra; she was seized on her alms-round, washed in the royal bath-house, provided with perfumes, chaplets, raiment and brilliant ornaments, and conducted to the king, who fell passionately in love with her. Utpalavarna, sent to see after her, instructed her in magic; and when the king, aroused from sleep, wished to embrace her, she raised herself heavenward - fear came upon him, he uttered cries of anguish, asked whether she was a goddess, a Nagi, a Yakshini or a Rakshasi, and fell at her feet begging the forgiveness she granted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahakasyapa and Bhadra (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Utpalavarna, the Blue-Lotus-Colored One

region.en: Takshasila, caravan road to Mathura (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 呾叉始羅與往馬土臘的商路（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. X, Utpalavarna (Kah-gyur viii. 216-273)

summary.en: Born with blue-lotus eyes and a lotus fragrance, Utpalavarna is married to a foundling son-in-law; discovering her own mother and husband in adultery on the day of her confinement, she hurls her newborn daughter at him, leaves, is taken to wife by a caravan-leader, and later unknowingly weds her own grown daughter - recognizing her by the scar from the fall on the threshold. Twice over she must flee a house where she has become mother and joint-wife at once.
summary.zh: 鄔缽羅華色天生青蓮眼與蓮香，招贅孤兒為婿；分娩之日撞見母親與丈夫私通，怒擲新生女兒，負氣離家，被商隊首領娶為妻——後來竟又不知情地嫁了自己的女兒，從其頭上的傷疤相認。兩度淪為「既為母又為共妻」，兩度出走。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; the tale's kinship transgressions are the narrative's subject-matter, reported factually.

passages.text: Just on the point of being confined, Utpalavarna sent her maid to call her mother and found her with her son-in-law; the maid, disbelieved, made the matter manifest by calling her in to see the two together. In wrath she cried, henceforth do what you please with her! - flung her new-born daughter at her husband, and the babe, glancing off his body, fell on the threshold and wounded its head; Utpalavarna veiled herself and left the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Utpalavarna (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: A caravan-leader enamoured of her beauty took her to wife; back in Takshasila for goods, he was persuaded to fetch as second wife a Gandhara woman exactly matching his description - his own daughter. Dressing the girl's hair, Utpalavarna found the scar on her head and asked its cause: my mother once tossed me to my father in a fit of passion, and I fell upon the threshold. As there she had been mother and joint-wife, and here her daughter was joint-wife, she veiled her head and departed again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Utpalavarna (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Utpalavarna Beguiles the Young Grocer

region.en: Grocers' quarter of Vaisali (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 吠舍離糧商街（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. X, Utpalavarna

summary.en: In Vaisali the courtesans lay a wager that whoever beguiles the unallured young grocer Anishtaprapta shall be their mistress. Utpalavarna has her maid buy perfumes and then sickness-daily-drugs 'for a young man of good family', paid from her own purse, until the grocer, moved, begs admittance - which she refuses while 'he' lies ill, burns a grass man in the cemetery, and mourns outside his shop. Only in the park, with wine, does she crown and convoy the staggering grocer home past the astonished courtesans, who name her their mistress.
summary.zh: 吠舍離眾妓立誓：能誘得少年糧商阿尼私多波羅多者即為眾妓之主。華色命侍女日日以「家中貴公子」之名購香藥、苦藥，實情皆是自掏腰包；糧商感動求見，她卻以「公子病重」屢拒，又於屍林焚草人、披髮痛哭過其門。終於在園林酒宴之後，她為醉倒的糧商戴上花冠攜回，眾妓驚嘆，尊其為主。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The maid bought perfumes daily, then bitter, acid and tart drugs, saying that a young man of good family had come to Utpalavarna's house and was ill - and that Utpalavarna paid from her own means. The grocer conceived a liking for her, begged a visit, and was told the young man was not yet cured; she burned a man's figure of grass in the cemetery and went wailing with dishevelled locks past his shop, and women, said the words of Bhagavant, enchain men in eight ways - by dancing, singing, playing, laughing, weeping, their appearance, their touch and their questions.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Utpalavarna (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the park the grocer brought quantities of food, drink, raiment and garlands; after they had eaten and drunk and he was no longer master of his senses, Utpalavarna set a wreath on his head, threw her arms round his neck, and convoyed him home. The courtesans cried that this Gandhara woman had splendidly beguiled the young grocer, and named her their mistress.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Utpalavarna (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Mother, Wife, Sister: Utpalavarna's Tangled House
title.zh: 母亦妻、女亦妹：華色亂家

region.en: Eastern and western gates of Vaisali (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 吠舍離東西兩門（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. X, Utpalavarna

summary.en: Utpalavarna abandons her newborn son at the eastern gate and her daughter at the western - and the two warders' households, old friends, raise them and marry them to each other. She herself, grown a courtesan of Vaisali, becomes concubine and then wife of the eastern warder's son. One Brahman's riddling verse forces the truth out of the maidservant: your son is now your husband, your daughter your fellow-wife - and only the power of Mahamaudgalyayana, soaring aloft like a flamingo-king out of her embrace, turns her from beguiling to asking for instruction in the doctrine.
summary.zh: 華色棄子於東門、棄女於西門；兩戶世交的門吏各自抱養，長大後結為夫婦。華色淪為吠舍離名妓，竟嫁與東門吏之子為妻。一婆羅門以謎語詩道破天機：妳的兒子如今是妳的丈夫，妳的女兒是妳的共妻——她再度出走。最後欲以擁抱魅惑目犍連，尊者如鷺王凌空而起，她轉而求教於法，得聞四諦。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; the kinship entanglement is the narrative's own theme, reported factually.

passages.text: The maid laid the child by the roadside near the eastern warder's house with a lamp beside it; the warder carried it in crying 'good wife, there is a son for you', and the western warder, hearing of it, sent raiment and ornaments for the future bride. Later the daughter was exposed at the western gate and raised by his wife, and the eastern warder sent her ornaments as his son's future wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Utpalavarna (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The grown son, dragooned by his companions into taking the courtesan Utpalavarna to the park under penalty of sixty Karshapanas, fell in love with her; the Licchavis consented to the marriage in consideration of his father's services, and the western warder's daughter was given him besides as the agreed wife. To her Mahamaudgalyayana cried: your fellow-wife is your mother, your husband is your brother. And when a Brahman's riddling verse forced the maid-servant to confess that the son exposed at the east gate was now Utpalavarna's husband and the daughter at the west gate her fellow-wife, Utpalavarna veiled her head and left the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Utpalavarna (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Rajagriha, leading her new life as a courtesan, she wagered five hundred Karshapanas that she could beguile even Mahamaudgalyayana; all her artifices failed, and when she tried to embrace him he soared aloft with outstretched wings like a flamingo-king. By the words he spoke she was so affected that she besought him to instruct her in the doctrine; he did so, and she recognised the four truths.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Utpalavarna (1882); not verbatim.
